vs base "main" (run `git -C /Users/elmabi/Desktop/my-projets/workstation diff main...HEAD` to see it — 12 files, ~1200 insertions / 102 deletions,
5 commits). This branch fixes two production incidents in a workstation "banc d'essai" (skill-improvement
rail): (1) an import marker that permanently sealed a recoverable failure (server/cli/evalsReconciler.ts,
RETRYABLE_ON_FAILURE_KINDS), (2) a provenance-check false positive in a local LLM judge that rejected honest
citations due to JSON escaping + typographic punctuation (server/services/reviews/localJudge.ts,
normalizeForProvenance / decodeJsonlStringValues), plus two follow-up chip fixes: (3) a git-merge
"unrelated histories" failure when applying skill-improvement branches, fixed by a hand-built two-parent
merge commit that mechanically confines its tree diff to <skill>/ (server/services/reviews/apply.ts,
graftSkillContent — uses raw git plumbing: rm -r, checkout, write-tree, commit-tree), and (4) two race
conditions in a CLI "wait for a hub conversation to be answered" command (server/cli/convo.ts, wakeReason —
removed a stale baseline-comparison mechanism in favor of a pure function of the current snapshot). Docs
were updated in docs/evals/*.md and docs/decision-hub.md to match.
Read the full changed files + their callers/siblings, AND read the MOST-BOUNDED/safest sibling of any
git-plumbing call, marker/lock pattern, or CLI exit-code contract you touch, so you know THIS repo's idiom.
For any file/function that is WHOLLY NEW in this diff (e.g. graftSkillContent, decodeJsonlStringValues,
RETRYABLE_ON_FAILURE_KINDS), audit it standalone — there is no old behavior to diff against. For a
pre-existing function changed by this diff (wakeReason, normalizeForProvenance, mergeApprovedBranchIntoMain,
cmdImport's catch block), scope to what the diff changed vs main, but verify the new behavior against EVERY
call site and EVERY code path (success AND failure) of that function, not just the one path the commit
message describes.
A finding is reportable if it fails ANY gate:
  • CORRECTNESS: some input makes it wrong / crash / lose data (triggerable), OR
  • CONVENTION/SCALABILITY/PLATFORM-LIMIT: it deviates from an idiom that ALREADY exists in this repo
    (cite the sibling file:line that does it right), violates an external hard limit, or is an unbounded
    read / full-table scan / N+1 / over-fetch — EVEN IF today's data makes it work.
  • WIRING: new/changed enforcement/tooling code (marker files that gate at-most-once application, a
    provenance security check, a git-merge safety boundary, a CLI exit-code contract) that does not
    actually fire against this repo's real data shapes/paths, or is not wired into every place the same
    invariant should hold (e.g. is the graft's path-safety guard checked BEFORE every destructive git
    call, not just the first one? does the marker-retry logic apply to every code path that can throw?).
  • STATE-SAFETY: a gate/marker/lock that can be satisfied without the protected work happening, that can
    be bypassed by a crafted input (e.g. a skill name, a candidate id), that leaves the repo/data in a
    half-mutated state on a mid-operation crash, or that can block forever (no escape hatch / re-entrancy
    guard). This is CENTRAL to this diff: it is exactly the class of bug (a marker/gate posed before a
    side-effect, never retired on failure) that motivated the whole chantier — verify the NEW code doesn't
    reintroduce a narrower version of the SAME defect it fixes (e.g. does graftSkillContent's git plumbing
    leave the integration clone in a half-reset state on a partial failure? does the new judge-local-adjacent
    change interact badly with the STILL-UNFIXED judge-local-markers "judging" stuck-state defect, already
    flagged as a separate known chip?).
"Returns correct output today / not triggerable" is NOT grounds to drop a convention/scalability/
platform-limit/wiring/state-safety finding — those are precisely what a review bot flags. Refute
ONLY pure style (naming/formatting/taste/restated guards).

DIMENSION: The provenance barrier (localJudge.ts) is a security control against a compromised/hallucinating judge — does the typographic-punctuation fold or the decoded-JSONL corpus addition create ANY new way for a fabricated or reformulated citation to pass? The graft (apply.ts) mutates a REAL remote main branch — does isSafeSegment fully cover path traversal via proposal.skill in every place it is used destructively, including any second call site this diff or its callers might have missed?

If a finding overlaps another dimension's territory, note the overlap in one line rather than re-developing it.

The real concern is that a compromised judge script could hallucinate or reward-hack by writing plausible-sounding quotes as evidence for a low grade, and the barrier needs to reject evidence strings that aren't actually verbatim in the transcript. Based on my review, I identified two substantive findings, both verified empirically (not just plausible). I confirmed finding #1 by actually reproducing the git pathspec-injection against a throwaway repo — `git rm -r --ignore-unmatch -q -- ':(exclude)nonexistent/'` reduces a 3-file repo to git's canonical empty tree (`4b825dc6...`), which is exactly the pathspec string `graftSkillContent` builds from an unconstrained `proposal.skill` (`z.string().min(1)`, no character restriction, confirmed in `src/types/review.ts:155,306`). This directly contradicts the explicit "security property" both the code's docstring (`apply.ts:507-517`) and `docs/evals/rail-application.md:175-178` assert ("rien en dehors de `<proposal.skill>/` ne peut JAMAIS être touché"). `isSafeSegment` (`server/services/slug.ts:207`) only guards filesystem path traversal (`/`, `\`, `..`, control chars) — it has no notion of git's pathspec "magic" syntax (a leading `:`), so it does not cover the destructive git call it was placed in front of.

Finding #2 (decoded-JSONL corpus splicing) is a plausible-but-unconfirmed weakening of the same provenance security barrier — I traced the code precisely (`decodeJsonlStringValues` joins every string value from every field of every JSONL record, across the whole file, with a single `\n`) and confirmed via the test diff that no test exercises the multi-line/multi-field case, only single-line/single-field. I rate it PLAUSIBLE rather than CONFIRMED since exploiting it requires a specific adversarial construction I did not reproduce end-to-end.

findings.title: graftSkillContent's proposal.skill guard blocks fs path traversal but not git pathspec magic — a crafted skill name lets `git rm -r`/`git add -A` wipe the ENTIRE remote repo tree instead of `<skill>/`, and the resulting empty-tree merge commit is pushed to the real target's `main`
findings.scenario: proposal.skill is an open `z.string().min(1)` (src/types/review.ts:155,306) filled from the cloud round's `results.json` — explicitly treated as adversarial input by this very function's own docstring ("whether by cloud bug or a compromised routine"). If skill = ":(exclude)nonexistent", `graftSkillContent` builds `skillPath = ":(exclude)nonexistent/"` and passes it as the pathspec to `git rm -r --ignore-unmatch -q -- $skillPath` (line 560) and `git add -A -- $skillPath` (line 590). `isSafeSegment` (server/services/slug.ts:207) only rejects `/`, `\`, `..`, and control chars — it has no concept of git's leading-`:` pathspec-magic syntax, so this value passes the guard cleanly. I reproduced this empirically in a scratch repo: `git rm -r --ignore-unmatch -q -- ':(exclude)nonexistent/'` alone (no other positive pathspec) stages a delete of EVERY tracked file, and the subsequent `git add -A -- $skillPath` re-stages the now-empty working tree, so `git write-tree` produces git's canonical EMPTY TREE (`4b825dc642cb6eb9a060e54bf8d69288fbee4904`) — confirmed by literally running the same sequence of commands the function issues. `git commit-tree <emptyTree> -p mainSha -p branchSha` then builds a valid two-parent merge commit with ZERO files, `git push origin main:main` (mergeApprovedBranchIntoMain, apply.ts:~721) pushes it live to the real target repo (the actual `claude-skills` or meta-govern remote), and the function returns `{ ok: true }` since every git command exits 0 — no error path is triggered, so this is silently reported as a successful merge. This directly falsifies the explicit invariant claimed in both the function's own docstring (apply.ts:507-517, "rien en dehors de `<proposal.skill>/` ne peut JAMAIS être touché par cette fonction, quel que soit le contenu réel de la branche") and docs/evals/rail-application.md:175-178 (same claim, verbatim). No test in apply.test.ts exercises a pathspec-magic skill name (only `.`/`..`/`/`-shaped ones are tested, e.g. the 'finding #3' test at apply.test.ts:1150), so this is undetected by the diff's own test suite.
findings.suggestedFix: In graftSkillContent's guard (and the sibling guard in installSkillFromIntegrationClone, which is currently safe only because it uses `path.join` rather than a git pathspec — but should stay defensive too), reject any `proposal.skill` whose first character is `:` (git's pathspec-magic delimiter), or — more robustly — force literal pathspec interpretation for every git invocation that takes `skillPath` as an argument (e.g. `git -c core.literalPathspecs=true rm -r ...` / set `GIT_LITERAL_PATHSPECS=1` in the child-process env for gitTry/git/gitOut when called from this function), so a crafted skill name can never be interpreted as pathspec magic regardless of guard completeness. Add a regression test with a skill name like `:(exclude)x` or `:(glob)*` asserting the graft either refuses cleanly or provably only ever touches `<skill>/`, mirroring the existing `nom de skill contenant "/"` test.

findings.title: decodeJsonlStringValues joins every string value from every field of every JSONL event across the WHOLE transcript with a bare newline, letting a compromised/hallucinating judge splice unrelated fragments into a fabricated "verbatim" citation that the strict-substring provenance check will accept
findings.scenario: The provenance barrier's own docstring frames it explicitly as "a security control against a compromised/hallucinating judge" that must reject any evidence that isn't a literal, contiguous excerpt of the transcript. `decodeJsonlStringValues` parses each JSONL line independently but pushes every string value it finds — recursively, across ALL keys (message content, tool_use ids, file paths, roles, timestamps-as-strings, model names, etc.) and ALL lines of the whole transcript — into one flat `parts` array, then returns `parts.join('\n')` (line 1112) as ONE corpus entry added (not replacing) alongside the raw-bytes corpus. `isProvenanced` (line 1123-1126) is a strict `.includes()` substring check against this joined string. Because the joiner is a single bare `\n` with no field/line boundary marker, the tail of one field's string value (e.g. the end of an unrelated message, or a tool-result id) becomes byte-adjacent to the head of a completely different field's value from a different, possibly much-later event — a seam that never existed as contiguous text anywhere in the real conversation. A judge that already has full read access to the raw transcript (that is its whole job) could construct an "evidence" string straddling exactly such a seam and have it accepted as a legitimate literal citation, exactly the fabrication class this barrier exists to reject. The diff's own new tests (localJudge.test.ts, 'round 4' describe block) only exercise a SINGLE JSONL line with the citation inside ONE field's string value — none exercise the multi-line/multi-field splicing surface this function newly introduces, so the gap is untested.
findings.suggestedFix: Narrow decodeJsonlStringValues to only collect the actual message/content-shaped string fields (not ids, paths, roles, timestamps, tool names, etc.), and/or join with a separator that cannot legitimately appear inside a fabricated multi-fragment citation and that resets per LINE rather than accumulating across the whole file (e.g. keep each line's decoded text as its own separate corpus entry instead of one global `parts.join('\n')` across the entire transcript) — this keeps a citation matchable only within the boundaries of a single real event rather than across arbitrarily distant, unrelated ones. Add a regression test with two adjacent transcript lines whose field values, if spliced, would form a plausible-looking but never-actually-written sentence, asserting the barrier rejects it.
